full_prose_under_review.title: Schedule III-V Refills and Massachusetts Transfers
learning_objectives: Apply both the issue-date clock and refill-count limit to Schedule III and IV prescriptions.
Separate transfer eligibility from the prescription's remaining lawful refill capacity.
Recognize the special Massachusetts treatment of Schedule VI transfers.
Separate the federal one-time limit on a Schedule III-V refill transfer from the Massachusetts duty to transfer at the patient's request.
Identify who may execute a transfer, and separate the initial-dispensing electronic transfer from the refill-purpose transfer.

quick_review.text: Federal law bars filling or refilling a Schedule III or IV prescription more than six months after the issue date and bars more than five refills; only a new prescription lifts either limit.

For pharmacies subject to 247 CMR 9.04(13), a Massachusetts Schedule V prescription may not be filled or refilled more than six months after issue, and may not be refilled more than five times; that subsection does not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.
Massachusetts requires a timely patient-requested transfer, prohibits a transfer fee, and permits a pharmacy to act as the patient's agent to obtain the transfer.

Transfer of Schedule III-V prescription information for refill purposes is permitted between pharmacies on a one-time basis only, unless the pharmacies electronically share a real-time, online database.

Transfer of an unfilled electronic controlled-substance prescription for initial dispensing is a separate federal pathway, permitted between retail pharmacies at the patient's request on a one-time basis only, and it reaches Schedules II through V.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule III or IV refill is requested.
decision_logic.action: Check both elapsed time from issue and the number of prior refills; either exhausted limit blocks the refill.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts Schedule V refill is requested at a pharmacy subject to 247 CMR 9.04(13).
decision_logic.action: Apply the five-refill and six-month limits independently.

decision_logic.condition: The facility is an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Do not apply the Schedule V refill limits in 247 CMR 9.04(13) through this provision; 247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes that facility type.

decision_logic.condition: A patient or authorized agent requests a Massachusetts prescription transfer.
decision_logic.action: Transfer remaining authorized refills timely without charging a transfer fee, subject to the prescription-specific limits.

decision_logic.condition: A patient asks to move a Schedule III, IV or V prescription with authorized refills remaining to another pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the prescription has not already been transferred once, unless the two pharmacies electronically share a real-time online database, before applying the Massachusetts transfer duty.

decision_logic.condition: A patient asks a retail pharmacy to move an ELECTRONIC controlled-substance prescription that has never been dispensed to another retail pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Use the initial-dispensing electronic transfer pathway rather than the refill-transfer rule, keep the prescription in electronic form and unaltered, and treat it as available once only. A never-dispensed paper prescription has no federal transfer pathway.

ma_vs_federal.text: For Schedule III and IV refills the federal five-refill and six-month limits remain operative when the Massachusetts transfer rules are applied, and so does the separate federal limit permitting a Schedule III-V refill-purpose transfer only once.

Massachusetts Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedule III-V prescriptions and may move up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, with the only ceiling being that a refill-authorising Schedule VI prescription may not be transferred more than one year after issue. The federal one-time limit does not cap them, because it reaches only federally scheduled III, IV and V substances and a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug is by definition in no other schedule.

A federal controlled-prescription transfer must pass directly between two licensed pharmacists, while Massachusetts lets a certified pharmacy technician do the work for Schedule VI only, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

exceptions.text: A transfer does not create new refill authority or restart an issue-date clock.
The Schedule V refill limits in 247 CMR 9.04(13) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies under 247 CMR 9.04(15).
Pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization instead of the one-time limit.
The real-time shared-database allowance belongs to the refill-purpose transfer rule; the initial-dispensing electronic transfer carries no such counterpart and stays one-time.

timing_deadlines.consequence: No further fill or refill after the federal time limit without practitioner renewal.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts Schedule V refill window at a pharmacy subject to 247 CMR 9.04(13)
timing_deadlines.consequence: No first fill and no refill after the state time limit, and no refill once five are used.

timing_deadlines.event: Remaining-refill transfer of a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 1 year after issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) does not permit that remaining-refill transfer after the one-year point.

role_duties.duty: Obtain the patient-requested transfer and preserve the remaining lawful refill limits.

Transfer the prescription at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay therapy, and complete the federal voiding and transfer records for a Schedule III-V refill transfer.
Communicate a federal controlled-prescription transfer directly between the two of them; the transfer is a pharmacist-to-pharmacist act.
Perform a prescription transfer only for Schedule VI, and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

common_traps.text: Starting a six-month clock at the first dispensing rather than the issue date gives the prescription excess life.
Assuming a transfer renews or expands refill authority confuses movement of a prescription with creation of a new prescription.
Treating the Massachusetts duty to transfer on patient request as removing the federal one-time limit on a Schedule III-V refill transfer.
Concluding that a Schedule II prescription can never move between pharmacies overlooks the one-time initial-dispensing transfer of an unfilled electronic prescription.
Letting a certified pharmacy technician transfer a Schedule III-V prescription ignores both the Schedule VI limit on that authority and the federal pharmacist-to-pharmacist requirement.
Reading the Massachusetts Schedule V six-month limit as reaching only refills would let a seven-month-old prescription be dispensed for the first time.
Carrying the federal one-time transfer limit across to a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription refuses a second transfer the regulation allows.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A Schedule III or IV prescription may not be filled or refilled more than six months after its issue date and may not be refilled more than five times unless renewed by the practitioner.

authority.name: Transfer between pharmacies of prescription information for Schedules III, IV, and V controlled substances for refill purposes

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Transfer of original prescription information for a controlled substance listed in Schedule III, IV or V for the purpose of refill dispensing is permissible between pharmacies ON A ONE-TIME BASIS ONLY; pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may instead transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization. The transfer must be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists, the transferring pharmacist must void and annotate the original record, and the receiving pharmacist must record the required transfer data. The procedure is permissible only if allowable under existing State or other applicable law, and it moves the prescription without creating new refill authority or restarting the six-month issue-date clock.
exceptions: Pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization.
The transfer procedure is permissible only if allowable under existing State or other applicable law.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A Massachusetts Schedule V prescription may not be refilled more than five times or later than six months after the prescription was issued.

authority.name: Certified pharmacy technician Schedule VI transfer scope

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under current 247 CMR 9.14, a pharmacy must timely transfer a prescription at the request of the patient or authorized agent, may act as the patient's agent to obtain the transfer, and may not charge a transfer fee. Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedule III-V prescriptions; remaining authorized refills may be transferred, but a Schedule VI prescription may not be transferred more than one year after issuance. Under 247 CMR 8.04, a certified pharmacy technician may perform a Schedule VI transfer with approval of the pharmacist on duty.
exceptions: Schedule-specific federal requirements may add restrictions for federally controlled prescriptions; do not automatically import those mechanics into a Massachusetts Schedule VI transfer.

authority.name: One-time transfer of electronic controlled prescriptions

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: At a patient's request, an unfilled electronic Schedule II through V prescription may be transferred once between DEA-registered retail pharmacies if allowed by state law, kept electronic, unaltered, and communicated directly between pharmacists.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Massachusetts Schedule VI includes prescription drugs not otherwise placed in Schedules I through V; Schedule VI status does not itself make a drug federally controlled or routinely MassPAT-reportable.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

full_prose_under_review.title: Massachusetts Schedule VI
learning_objectives: Recognize Schedule VI as a Massachusetts prescription-drug classification rather than a federal controlled schedule.
Apply Massachusetts prescription elements, oral documentation, electronic-prescribing exceptions, and transfer rules without inventing federal consequences.
Apply the Schedule VI validity clock and the additional-drug consequences instead of treating Schedule VI as a consequence-free label.
Recognise that the Schedule VI classification carries its own scope-of-practice consequence for who may transfer a prescription.

quick_review.text: Massachusetts Schedule VI includes prescription drugs not otherwise placed in Massachusetts Schedules I through V.
Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement, while all other validity requirements remain applicable.
An oral controlled-substance prescription must be reduced to writing immediately with the required information; the separate duty to deliver a later follow-up prescription does not reach Schedule VI.
A Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill it after one year.
A Schedule VI drug the Department designates as an additional drug becomes reportable to the prescription monitoring program and requires a customer identifier at dispensing.
Schedule VI is the only schedule for which a certified pharmacy technician may perform a prescription transfer, and then only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

A Schedule VI prescription may be transferred up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized; the federal one-time transfer limit does not reach it, because Schedule VI is not a federal schedule.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription drug is not in Massachusetts Schedules I-V.
decision_logic.action: Classify it under Schedule VI, then identify the separate rule governing validity, documentation, dispensing, or transfer.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule VI prescription is written or oral rather than electronic.
decision_logic.action: Do not reject it solely for that format; apply the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception and all remaining prescription requirements, including the form requirements that still govern a written prescription.

decision_logic.condition: A patient requests transfer of a Schedule VI prescription with authorized refills remaining.
decision_logic.action: Use the remaining-refill transfer pathway under 247 CMR 9.14(4): the prescription may move up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, that regulation bars transfer more than one year after issue, and a certified pharmacy technician may carry out the transfer with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule VI prescription is presented more than one year after its issue date, or with no refills remaining and the prescriber cannot be reached in time.
decision_logic.action: Do not refill it; consider only the professional-judgment continuation of a quantity not exceeding 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging.

decision_logic.condition: The Schedule VI medication being dispensed has been designated an additional drug by the Department.
decision_logic.action: Obtain a customer identifier and treat the dispensing as reportable, using the documented hardship route only on its own terms.

ma_vs_federal.text: Schedule VI is a Massachusetts classification and does not itself make a drug federally controlled.
A Schedule VI drug the Department designates as an additional drug carries Massachusetts prescription-monitoring and customer-identifier duties that the Schedule VI label alone does not imply.

exceptions.text: The Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception removes that format mandate, not the required prescription elements or oral documentation duties.

Where a Schedule VI prescription has expired or has no remaining refills and prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner, the pharmacist may in professional judgment dispense a quantity not exceeding 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging.

247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(12), and from 9.04(10) and 9.04(14) as well, so the Schedule VI validity clock, the day-counting convention and the customer-identifier duty all fall away for that facility type.
In deciding whether a prescription is within date the pharmacist counts the day after it was written as day one, so the Schedule VI one-year period does not include the issue date itself.

The follow-up duty Schedule VI escapes is the practitioner's obligation to deliver an electronic prescription within 2 days, or a written one within not more than 7 days where the prescriber holds an electronic-prescribing exception.

timing_deadlines.event: Remaining-refill transfer of a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 1 year after issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) does not permit that remaining-refill transfer after the regulatory one-year limit.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: 1 year from the date of issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: A licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year.

forms_records.text: The pharmacist must immediately reduce an oral controlled-substance prescription to writing with the required Massachusetts prescription information.
A customer identifier must be obtained when dispensing a Schedule VI additional drug; the hardship route requires a documented reason and the recipient's printed and signed name and address.

A written Schedule VI prescription must carry the practitioner's signature and must either be transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or be written on a tamper-resistant form consistent with federal Medicaid requirements; a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and may not be filled.

role_duties.duty: Validate required prescription elements even when the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception applies.
Check the Schedule VI validity clock and any additional-drug designation before dispensing rather than treating Schedule VI as consequence-free.
Perform a prescription transfer only for Schedule VI, and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

common_traps.text: Reading the electronic-prescribing exception as an exemption from all prescription validity requirements is incorrect.
Treating Schedule VI as a federal schedule creates legal consequences that the Massachusetts classification does not supply.

The one-year rule in 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) governs transfer of a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills and is separate from the one-year prescription validity limit in 247 CMR 9.04(12); neither should be restated as the other.
Concluding that Schedule VI never triggers identification or monitoring-program duties overlooks Schedule VI drugs designated as additional drugs.
Generalising the certified-technician transfer authority beyond Schedule VI ignores the word only in the regulation.
Reading the electronic-prescribing exception as removing every format requirement leaves the pharmacist filling a written prescription that no permitted format supports.

exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Massachusetts requirements for dispensing and refilling prescriptions

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 9.04(12) a prescription for a Schedule VI medication is valid for ONE YEAR from the date of issue and a licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year. If a Schedule VI prescription expires or has no remaining refills and the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner, the pharmacist in his or her professional judgment may dispense a quantity NOT TO EXCEED 14 DAYS or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging. Under 247 CMR 9.04(15) the requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(12) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.
exceptions: 247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(12).
The continuation supply is a professional-judgment allowance conditioned on inability to obtain timely prescriber authorization; it is not an automatic refill.

authority.name: Standards for prescription format and security in Massachusetts
DCP Electronic Prescribing and Dispensing Manual

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Massachusetts generally requires covered prescriptions to be issued electronically subject to 105 CMR 721.070 exceptions and waivers. Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the state electronic-prescribing requirement under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9). Under 105 CMR 721.070(C), a pharmacist who receives an otherwise valid written or oral prescription is not required to verify that the prescription properly falls within an electronic-prescribing exception or waiver; all other prescription and controlled-substance requirements still apply.
exceptions: Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9).
Other enumerated exceptions and waivers may permit a covered prescription to be issued in written or oral form.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: On receiving an oral prescription for a controlled substance, the pharmacist must immediately reduce it to writing with the information required by M.G.L. c. 94C §20 and make a reasonable effort to authenticate an unfamiliar prescriber; the subsection requiring later electronic or written documentation expressly does not apply to Schedule VI.
exceptions: The follow-up prescription requirement in §20(c) does not apply to Schedule VI, but immediate reduction to writing and validity duties still apply.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A controlled-substance prescription must include the practitioner, patient, drug, strength, directions, date, registration, cautionary, and refill information required by Massachusetts law.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Massachusetts Department of Public Health regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: The Commissioner MAY DETERMINE that a drug is an 'additional drug' for the purposes of 105 CMR 700.012 because it carries a BONA FIDE POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE, based on factors including a risk of addiction alone or with a Schedule II through IV drug, known recreational use, known regular diversion for misuse, or a known contribution to overdose or regular presence in the bloodstream of persons who have overdosed. UPON MAKING SUCH A DETERMINATION THE COMMISSIONER SHALL NOTIFY ALL DISPENSERS THAT THEY MUST BEGIN TO REPORT the dispensing of that additional drug pursuant to prescription as directed in 105 CMR 700.012(A).

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A licensee shall require a CUSTOMER IDENTIFIER, being the identification number on a valid government issued identification obtained by inspecting the identification of the ultimate user or their agent, on dispensing a controlled substance in Schedules II through V or an additional drug under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1). A licensee may dispense WITHOUT one only if it has reason to believe that refusing would cause SERIOUS HARDSHIP to the ultimate user or agent AND DOCUMENTS THE REASON, AND the recipient PRINTS name and address on the reverse of the prescription or in a prescription log AND SIGNS it. The Commissioner may waive or modify the requirement for refills, deliveries or other specified activities.
exceptions: Documented serious hardship with the recipient's printed name, address and signature
Commissioner waiver or modification for refills, deliveries or other specified activities

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: In order to determine whether a prescription is WITHIN DATE, a pharmacist shall count the DAY AFTER the prescription was written as DAY ONE. The issue date itself is not counted, so a period measured in days runs from the following day.

authority.name: Commissioner exceptions permitting written and oral prescriptions
Follow-up documentation for an oral prescription issued under an ePrescribing exception

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) a practitioner who prescribes a controlled substance by oral prescription shall cause an ELECTRONIC prescription to be delivered to the dispensing pharmacy WITHIN 2 DAYS; if the practitioner has received an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner under s. 23(h), the practitioner shall instead cause a WRITTEN prescription to be delivered within not more than 7 DAYS, or the shorter period required by federal law, postmarked within that period. The follow-up prescription must indicate that it documents an oral prescription, and the pharmacy attaches it to the oral prescription it reduced to writing. Under 105 CMR 721.070(B) a practitioner issuing an oral prescription for a controlled substance in SCHEDULES II THROUGH V under a 105 CMR 721.070(A) ePrescribing exception shall cause a written or electronic prescription to be delivered within not more than SEVEN BUSINESS DAYS, or the shorter period required by federal law. The s. 20(c) requirements do not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI.
exceptions: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) does not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI, although the immediate reduction to writing and the remaining validity duties still apply.
A shorter federal period controls where federal law requires one, such as the 7-day emergency oral Schedule II follow-up under 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4).

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Where state and federal law permit a WRITTEN prescription, 105 CMR 721.020(F) requires it to be issued on a form carrying the practitioner's signature and to be EITHER transmitted via facsimile or similar technology OR written on a TAMPER-RESISTANT FORM consistent with federal requirements for Medicaid. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(i) states the same at statute level. Under 105 CMR 721.040(A) a prescription in a format that does not conform is INVALID AND SHALL NOT BE FILLED. An exception that permits a written prescription therefore removes the electronic-format mandate only; the written form requirements continue to govern the prescription the exception allows.
exceptions: The facsimile route and the tamper-resistant form route are alternatives; either satisfies 105 CMR 721.020(F)(1)-(2).

full_prose_under_review.title: Massachusetts Oral Prescriptions and the Electronic-Prescribing Exceptions
full_prose_under_review.topic: Controlled prescriptions / Oral prescriptions and format exceptions
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Oral receipt, follow-up documentation, and the out-of-state oral pathway
learning_objectives: Carry out the pharmacist's duties at the moment an oral controlled-substance prescription is received.
Choose the correct follow-up period by identifying which authority governs the prescriber's obligation.
Apply the out-of-state oral Schedule III-V pathway with its own validity limit and verification gate.

quick_review.text: On receiving an oral controlled-substance prescription the pharmacist must immediately reduce it to writing with the information Massachusetts requires, and must make a reasonable effort to authenticate a prescriber who is not known to the pharmacist.

The prescriber's follow-up is an electronic prescription within 2 days, or a written one within not more than 7 days where the prescriber holds an electronic-prescribing exception; that duty does not reach Schedule VI.

Massachusetts generally requires covered prescriptions to be issued electronically, and a pharmacist receiving an otherwise valid written or oral prescription is not required to verify that it properly falls within an exception or waiver.

An out-of-state practitioner's Schedule III through VI prescription may be filled in Massachusetts only within 30 days of issue, and a Schedule III through V prescription must be verified by the pharmacist before it is filled.
A Failover counts as an oral prescription and requires no written or electronic follow-up, but only where all three of its conditions hold and the drug is not an additional drug.

decision_logic.condition: An oral controlled-substance prescription is received by telephone.
decision_logic.action: Reduce it to writing immediately with the required Massachusetts information, and authenticate the prescriber if that practitioner is not known to you.

decision_logic.condition: The prescriber issued the oral prescription and holds no electronic-prescribing exception.
decision_logic.action: Expect an electronic follow-up prescription within 2 days rather than a written one within 7.

decision_logic.condition: The oral Schedule III-V prescription came from an out-of-state practitioner.
decision_logic.action: Confirm it was issued within the preceding 30 days, verify it by telephone or other means, do not fill it if verification cannot be obtained, and record that you requested the written prescription.

decision_logic.condition: A technological or electrical failure prevented electronic transmission.
decision_logic.action: Treat a qualifying Failover as an oral prescription needing no follow-up, but only after checking all three conditions, including that the drug is not an additional drug.

ma_vs_federal.text: The Massachusetts follow-up periods run on the prescribing practitioner and are measured from the oral authorization, and a shorter federal period controls where federal law imposes one.

exceptions.text: Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement, and the section 20(c) follow-up duty does not reach Schedule VI either.

105 CMR 721.070(B) states the follow-up period for an oral Schedule II-V prescription issued under an electronic-prescribing exception as not more than seven business days, which is not the same measure as the statutory seven days.
The three Failover conditions are conjunctive; failing any one, including the additional-drug condition, leaves the ordinary follow-up duty in place.

The 30-day window belongs to the Schedule III through VI out-of-state pathway. Massachusetts applies a five-day presentation window to out-of-state Schedule II prescriptions instead, so the figure does not carry across schedules.

A written follow-up prescription must itself satisfy the Massachusetts written-format rules; it carries the practitioner's signature and is either transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or written on a tamper-resistant form consistent with federal Medicaid requirements.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner electronic follow-up after an oral controlled-substance prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: This is the default; the 7-day written route requires a section 23(h) exception.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner written follow-up where the prescriber holds an electronic-prescribing exception
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 7 days, or 7 business days under 105 CMR 721.070(B)
timing_deadlines.consequence: The writing must be postmarked within the period, and a shorter federal period controls.

timing_deadlines.event: Validity of an out-of-state Schedule III-VI prescription filled in Massachusetts
timing_deadlines.consequence: Outside that window the pathway does not authorize the fill at all.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner delivery of an out-of-state oral Schedule III-V written follow-up
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 7 days or the shorter federal period
timing_deadlines.consequence: The period governs the practitioner's delivery or mailing, not the pharmacist's recording.

forms_records.text: The pharmacist immediately reduces the oral prescription to writing on a prescription form with the prescriber, patient, drug, directions, serial number and refill information Massachusetts requires.
On the out-of-state oral Schedule III-V pathway the pharmacist records having requested the practitioner's written prescription.

role_duties.duty: Reduce the oral prescription to writing at once, authenticate an unfamiliar prescriber, and refuse to fill an out-of-state Schedule III-V prescription you cannot verify.
Deliver the follow-up prescription within the period that applies to you, electronically within 2 days unless you hold an electronic-prescribing exception.

common_traps.text: Quoting a single seven-day figure for every Massachusetts oral controlled-substance follow-up misses the two-day electronic default and the seven-business-day regulatory period.
Treating the follow-up period as a deadline for the pharmacist reverses the timed event; the practitioner must deliver or mail the writing within it.
Filling an out-of-state Schedule III-V prescription on the federal six-month clock ignores the 30-day Massachusetts limit and the verification gate that govern that pathway.
Refusing an otherwise valid written or oral prescription because you cannot confirm which exception it was issued under reverses the rule; the pharmacist is not required to verify that.
Calling any transmission failure a Failover skips the conditions, and an additional drug never qualifies.
Carrying the 30-day out-of-state window to a Schedule II prescription accepts one that Massachusetts allows only within five days of issue.

exceptions: The follow-up prescription requirement in §20(c) does not apply to Schedule VI, but immediate reduction to writing and validity duties still apply.

exceptions: Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9).
Other enumerated exceptions and waivers may permit a covered prescription to be issued in written or oral form.

authority.name: Failover treated as an oral prescription

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 105 CMR 721.020(G) a Failover SHALL BE CONSIDERED AN ORAL PRESCRIPTION and SHALL NOT REQUIRE a written or electronic follow-up prescription, provided all three conditions hold: the prescription contains everything M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires except the practitioner's signature and is immediately entered into a compliant electronic pharmacy system or otherwise reduced to writing by the dispensing pharmacist; if the prescribing practitioner is not known to the dispensing pharmacist, that pharmacist makes a reasonable good faith effort to determine the Failover was issued by a prescribing practitioner; and the prescription is NOT FOR AN ADDITIONAL DRUG as defined in 105 CMR 700.001. Under 105 CMR 721.040(C) an electronic prescription transmitted by other means is invalid except in the event of a Failover verified under 721.020(G).
exceptions: The three conditions in 105 CMR 721.020(G)(1)-(3) are conjunctive; failing any one leaves the ordinary follow-up duty in place.
A Failover for an Additional Drug does not qualify, so the follow-up duty continues to apply to it.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Massachusetts applies a five-day presentation window and different issuing-state conditions to out-of-state narcotic and nonnarcotic Schedule II prescriptions.

Where state and federal law permit a WRITTEN prescription, 105 CMR 721.020(F) requires it to be issued on a form carrying the practitioner's signature and to be EITHER transmitted via facsimile or similar technology OR written on a TAMPER-RESISTANT FORM consistent with federal requirements for Medicaid. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(i) states the same at statute level. Under 105 CMR 721.040(A) a prescription in a format that does not conform is INVALID AND SHALL NOT BE FILLED. An exception that permits a written prescription therefore removes the electronic-format mandate only; the written form requirements continue to govern the prescription the exception allows.
exceptions: The facsimile route and the tamper-resistant form route are alternatives; either satisfies 105 CMR 721.020(F)(1)-(2).
